intro:
This track follows a card payment after the café's till has recorded it, as messages carry it from the program that wrote it to every program that needs it: the ledger, the texting program, the nightly payouts. Lessons start from scenes everyone knows, such as a kitchen rail of order slips, a notebook you only ever add to, a bookmark left behind or a drink called out once. Then they open up the machinery, on a real Kafka broker running on your laptop.

Every message system is built on one of two designs, and the track builds both. The first is the **queue**: a broker, a program in the middle, hands each message to one reader and deletes it once the reader says it's done. The second is the **log**: the broker keeps every message in order, and each reader keeps one number, its place. Kafka, a program that keeps logs of messages for other programs to read, is the log the track takes apart, in version 4.4. By the end, you can:

- tell a queue from a log, and pick one for a job;
- explain how Kafka splits a log into partitions and files, keeps copies on several servers and deletes old data;
- choose a key so that one account's payments stay in order, and tune how a producer batches and retries;
- read with a consumer group, save your place at the right moment, and survive a rebalance;
- move a record that always fails out of the way without losing it;
- make a program's output and its bookmark one Kafka transaction, and say where exactly-once ends;
- let many readers share a partition with a share group, size partitions and read lag;
- use Redis pub/sub and Redis Streams, a lighter log kept in memory, and recover a crashed worker's messages.

The twelve lessons:

1. Queues and brokers: acknowledgements, redelivery and fan-out
2. The log: Kafka's one big idea
3. Partitions and segments on disk: retention and compaction
4. The cluster: KRaft, replicas and the ISR
5. Producers I: keys, partitions and ordering
6. Producers II: batching, acks and idempotence
7. Consumers: the poll loop, offsets and delivery guarantees
8. Consumer groups and rebalancing
9. Failure handling: poison pills, retries and dead letters
10. Transactions and exactly-once
11. Share groups and running Kafka in production
12. A lighter log: Redis pub/sub and Streams

You need to read a little code in Java and Kotlin (every sample comes in both), and to have JDK 21 or newer and Docker on your laptop. Docker is a free program that runs small, separate systems, called containers, on your own computer. You don't need any messaging background: every term is explained the first time a lesson uses it. When a lesson borrows an idea from an earlier track, such as copies and leaders (Replication), two-phase commit (Transactions) or fencing tokens (Faults, time and truth), it explains it again in a line.

The labs for lessons 1 to 11 are in `labs/kafka`, one package per lesson (`sfz.msg.l01` to `sfz.msg.l11`); lesson 12's lab is in `labs/redis` (`sfz.msg.l12`). Each lab builds a small model of the mechanism, such as a queue, a log, a set of in-sync copies, a transactional partition or a share partition. From lesson 2 on, it also builds a client that the tests run against a real Kafka 4.4 broker or Redis 8.10 server, which Testcontainers, a library that starts containers for tests, brings up for you. Where no broker is needed, the tests use `MockConsumer` and `MockProducer`, stand-ins that run in memory. Run `./gradlew :kafka:test --tests 'sfz.msg.lNN.*'` from the `labs` folder (`:redis:` for lesson 12) until it passes. The Try-its use `labs/env/kafka.yml` (one broker on `localhost:9092`), `labs/env/kafka-cluster.yml` (three brokers) and `labs/env/redis.yml`, and `./gradlew :kafka:demo -Pmain=...` runs the demos.
cheatsheet:
## Two designs (lessons 1, 2 and 11)

A queue hands out messages and forgets them. A log keeps them, and lets each reader keep its own place. RabbitMQ, a popular broker built around queues, is the queue example; its main kind of queue, the quorum queue, keeps copies on several servers.

| | Queue (RabbitMQ quorum queue) | Log read by a consumer group (Kafka) | Log read by a share group (Kafka 4.2+) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Progress kept as | a state per message | one saved offset per group and partition | a state per record in flight |
| After success | the message is deleted | the record stays until retention | the record stays until retention |
| How many readers can help | any number | at most one per partition | any number |
| Order | lost once a message is redelivered and two readers share the queue | kept per partition, so per key | lost |
| A reader goes quiet | its messages come back when its connection closes | its partitions move after the group's timeouts | each record's lock runs out (30 s) |
| A message that always fails | delivery limit 20, then dropped or dead-lettered | blocks its partition until your code acts | delivery limit 5, then archived or copied to a `dlq.` topic (4.4) |
| Reading again, or a second reader | needs its own queue, from now on | any group, from any offset | yes: it's still a log |

Queue facts. The reader acknowledges each message, which says it's done. Deliveries not yet acknowledged go back to the queue when the reader goes away, marked as redelivered, and that reorders messages once there are two readers. Prefetch caps how many unacknowledged messages one reader may hold. Auto-ack, acknowledging on delivery, is at-most-once. An exchange copies a message into every queue whose binding, a rule that joins the exchange to a queue, matches: fan-out across queues, load sharing inside one. Quorum queues dead-letter at-most-once by default.

## The log on disk (lessons 2 and 3)

A topic is a named log, split into partitions. A partition is a log you only add to at the end: the broker gives each record the next offset, offsets never change, and order exists only inside a partition. A reader's state is one number per partition, the offset of the next record to read. A consumer group saves it in `__consumer_offsets` as its committed offset. Reading deletes nothing.

| On disk | Rule |
|---|---|
| Segment | one of the files a partition is stored in, named by its first offset (`.log`, `.index`, `.timeindex`); only the newest, active segment takes new records; a new one starts at `segment.bytes` (1 GiB) or `segment.ms` (7 days) |
| Retention (`cleanup.policy=delete`) | deletes whole closed segments once their newest record is older than `retention.ms` (7 days), or the partition is over `retention.bytes`; the earliest offset jumps a segment at a time |
| Compaction (`cleanup.policy=compact`) | keeps at least the last record for each key in closed segments; offsets and order never change; a tombstone, a record with an empty value, deletes its key after `delete.retention.ms` (1 day) |
| Tiered storage | `remote.storage.enable=true`: closed segments go to cheap cloud file storage, and `local.retention.ms` keeps the newest on the broker's disk; needs a plugin; not for compacted topics |

## The cluster (lesson 4)

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Broker, cluster | a server that runs Kafka; a cluster is several brokers working together |
| KRaft controllers | the brokers that keep the cluster's own records, such as who leads each partition, in a Raft log, `__cluster_metadata`; run 3 or 5; ZooKeeper is gone since Kafka 4.0 |
| Leader, followers | one copy of each partition, the leader, takes the writes; the other copies, the followers, fetch from it |
| ISR | the in-sync replicas: the copies that keep up; a follower drops out after `replica.lag.time.max.ms` (30 s) or when its broker is fenced |
| High watermark | the end of the shortest log in the ISR; readers only get records below it |
| `acks=all` | the producer waits for the current ISR, which can be the leader alone |
| `min.insync.replicas` | the floor for `acks=all` (default 1): below it, writes fail with `NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS`; for money, use 3 copies and a floor of 2 |

## Producing (lessons 5 and 6)

- The partition of a record with a key is a hash of the key: `(murmur2(key bytes) & 0x7fffffff) % partitions`. Same key, same partition, same order. Key payments by account id. Adding partitions later moves most keys.
- A record without a key goes in sticky runs of about `batch.size` to one partition at a time, steered away from slow brokers (KIP-794).
- `send()` adds the record to a batch and returns at once, with a Future for the result. A batch leaves when it's full (`batch.size`, 16 KB) or old enough (`linger.ms`, 5 ms since Kafka 4.0).
- Retries happen on their own until `delivery.timeout.ms` (2 min). A `TimeoutException` means unknown, not unwritten.
- Idempotence, on by default, gives each producer an id and each batch a sequence number, so the leader drops repeats of the producer's own retries. It needs `acks=all`, retries and at most 5 requests in flight; `acks=1` turns it off without a word.

## Consuming (lessons 7 to 9)

| Setting or fact | Value and meaning |
|---|---|
| Threads | one thread per consumer; only `wakeup()` may be called from another |
| Position and committed offset | position: the next offset `poll` returns, kept in memory; committed: the group's saved bookmark in `__consumer_offsets` |
| What a commit saves | the next offset to read, last handled + 1; one number covers everything before it |
| Commit after the work | at-least-once: a crash repeats records, so check an idempotency key in the same database transaction as the change |
| Commit before the work | at-most-once: a crash loses records |
| `enable.auto.commit` | `true` by default, every 5 s inside `poll`; at-least-once only if each batch is finished before the next `poll` |
| `auto.offset.reset` | `latest` by default, for a group with no committed offset |
| `max.poll.records` / `max.poll.interval.ms` | 500 / 5 min: miss the interval and the member leaves the group |
| Consumer group | the partitions shared out over its members, one owner per partition; moving a partition moves its owner and bookmark, never its data |
| Rebalance | eager (the default assignor list starts with Range) takes back every partition; cooperative moves only what must move; the new protocol, KIP-848 (`group.protocol=consumer`, not the 4.4 client default), lets the broker assign and each member catch up on its own |
| Handing a partition over | commit in `onPartitionsRevoked`; never commit in `onPartitionsLost` |
| Is a member alive? | the session timeout (45 s) catches a dead process, `max.poll.interval.ms` a stuck loop; `group.instance.id` keeps partitions through a restart |
| A record that always fails | it blocks its partition: a few retries with growing waits for failures that pass, a dead-letter topic with origin headers (wait for its ack, then commit) for those that don't, retry topics for long waits, and a parked key to keep one account's order |

## Transactions (lesson 10)

`transactional.id`, then `initTransactions()` (raises the epoch, a fencing token, and aborts what an older copy left open), `beginTransaction()`, the sends, `sendOffsetsToTransaction(offsets, consumer.groupMetadata())` and `commitTransaction()`. After an abort, seek back to the start of the batch.

| Two-phase commit | Kafka transaction |
|---|---|
| Coordinator | the transaction coordinator, one broker, with its notes in `__transaction_state` |
| Participants | the partitions written to, plus the group's partition of `__consumer_offsets` |
| Commit point | "prepare commit" written to `__transaction_state` |
| Phase two | COMMIT or ABORT markers, one offset each, in every participant |
| A participant left waiting | an open transaction: `read_committed` readers stop at the last stable offset |

Readers need `isolation.level=read_committed` (the default is `read_uncommitted`). Cost in Confluent's 2017 test: about 3% of a producer's throughput with 1 KB records and a transaction every 100 ms. A transaction covers Kafka writes and bookmarks only: calls to other services and database writes need idempotency keys or an outbox. KIP-939, which would let Kafka join a database's commit, hasn't shipped in 4.4.

## Share groups and running Kafka (lesson 11)

| Share group | Rule |
|---|---|
| Record states | available, acquired (locked to one member for `share.record.lock.duration.ms`, 30 s), acknowledged, archived |
| Answers | ACCEPT done, RELEASE try again, REJECT give up (archive), RENEW make the lock last longer (explicit mode) |
| Delivery limit | `share.delivery.count.limit` 5, then archived; copied to a `dlq.` topic with `share.version` 2 (4.4, may still change) |
| Start | `share.auto.offset.reset` is `latest` by default |
| Small clusters | under 3 brokers, set `share.coordinator.state.topic.replication.factor` and `.min.isr` to 1 |

Partitions: the larger of target / what one partition takes from producers and target / what one reader handles, plus growth. Lag: the log end offset minus the committed offset, per partition; alert on growth and on the age of the oldest record. Tiered storage (production-ready since 3.9) moves closed segments to cheap cloud file storage.

## Redis pub/sub and Streams (lesson 12)

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `PUBLISH` / `SUBSCRIBE` | at-most-once broadcast to whoever is connected; nothing stored |
| `XADD key * f v` | add an entry; its ID is `<ms>-<seq>`; `MAXLEN ~ n` or `MINID ~ id` trims |
| `XREAD BLOCK ms STREAMS key id` | read after your own position; every reader sees every entry |
| `XGROUP CREATE key g $ MKSTREAM` | a consumer group that starts at the end |
| `XREADGROUP GROUP g c STREAMS key >` | new entries, one consumer each, recorded in the pending entries list (PEL) until `XACK` |
| `XPENDING`, `XAUTOCLAIM` | look at idle pending entries, and take them over; the delivery count marks a poison message |
| `XACKDEL` / `XDELEX` (8.2) | acknowledge and delete; `KEEPREF`, `DELREF`, `ACKED` |
| `XREADGROUP ... CLAIM ms` (8.4) | idle pending entries first, then new ones |
| `XADD ... IDMP pid iid` (8.6) | drops a writer's repeated adds within a time window |
| `XNACK` (8.8) | hand pending entries back at once; SILENT, FAIL or FATAL sets the delivery count |

A stream is like one partition, kept in memory. Its copies on other servers catch up later, so a failover can lose entries Redis already confirmed.

## Versions this track assumes

Apache Kafka 4.4 (October 2026): KRaft only, `linger.ms=5`, idempotence on by default, the new consumer protocol available (`group.protocol=consumer`) but not the client default, share groups production-ready since 4.2. RabbitMQ 4.x quorum queues. Redis 8.10.
recap: Two questions sort any message system: what it keeps after a message is handled, and what it tracks for each reader. A queue tracks every message and deletes it once acknowledged; a log keeps everything and tracks one offset per reader.

A partition is a log you only add to, with offsets that never change, and order exists only inside a partition. Retention deletes whole segment files, compaction keeps the latest record for each key, and neither touches the active segment.
A write is safe once the in-sync copies (the ISR) have it. `acks=all` waits for the ISR, and `min.insync.replicas` says how small the ISR may get: 3 copies and a floor of 2 for money.

The key picks the partition, so key payments by account and choose the partition count up front. The idempotent producer, on by default, stops its own retries from repeating or reordering records; it doesn't catch your program sending the same payment twice.

Delivery guarantees come from when the reader saves its place: before the work is at-most-once, after it is at-least-once. Make the work idempotent with an idempotency key, stored in the same transaction as the change.

A consumer group shares a fixed set of partitions over its members. A rebalance moves owners and bookmarks; commit on revoke, prefer the new consumer protocol, and keep each batch well inside `max.poll.interval.ms`.

A record that always fails stops its whole partition, because nothing in a consumer group counts attempts. A few retries, a dead-letter topic written before the commit, and a parked key keep the rest flowing in order.

Kafka transactions are two-phase commit inside Kafka: a program's output and its bookmark become visible together to `read_committed` readers. Anything outside Kafka still needs an idempotency key or an outbox.

Share groups and Redis Streams consumer groups are queues built on logs: an answer per record and no order, but the records stay for other readers. Redis keeps its log in memory and leaves recovery and dead letters to your code.

quiz.q: Two readers share one RabbitMQ queue, and each acknowledges a message when it has handled it. Reader B crashes while it holds m3; reader A has already handled m4. What happens to the order of m3 and m4?
options: It's kept: the broker puts m3 back at its original place
It's broken: m3 is delivered again, so A handles it after m4
It's kept, because a queue is first in, first out
m3 is lost, because B crashed before acknowledging it
quiz.why: Deliveries that weren't acknowledged go back to the queue when the reader goes away, and m3 goes back to its old place. But A has already handled m4 by then, so the order of handling is m4, m3. Sharing a queue plus redelivery reorders messages: a queue is first in, first out only when it hands them out. Nothing is lost, because the broker kept m3 until it was acknowledged.

quiz.q: Which statement about Kafka's retention and compaction is true?
options: Retention deletes single records once they're too old
Compaction removes all but the last record for each key in every segment, including the active one
Retention deletes whole closed segments; compaction keeps the last record for each key in closed segments and never changes offsets
Compaction renumbers offsets so the log has no gaps
quiz.why: Both work on closed segments, the files a partition no longer adds to. Retention drops whole segments whose newest record is too old, so the earliest offset jumps a segment at a time. Compaction rewrites closed segments to keep the latest record for each key, leaving gaps in the offsets; the active segment is never cleaned. The tempting first option pictures records expiring one by one, which never happens.

quiz.q: A topic keeps 3 copies of each partition and the default `min.insync.replicas`. Both followers fall behind and leave the ISR, the set of copies that keep up. A producer with `acks=all` writes a payment, the leader confirms it, and then the leader's disk dies. What happened?
options: Nothing is lost: `acks=all` waits for all three copies
The producer would have got `NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS`, so it tried elsewhere
The followers copy the record from the controller
The payment can be lost: `acks=all` waited for the ISR, which was only the leader; `min.insync.replicas=2` would have refused the write
quiz.why: `acks=all` means every copy currently in the ISR, and the ISR can shrink to the leader alone. The default `min.insync.replicas` is 1, so the write was accepted with one copy. With 2, the leader would have refused it while the ISR was too small, and the producer would have known. The tempting first option reads "all" as all copies.

quiz.q: Every payment of one account must be applied in order. Which setup gives you that?
options: Key records by account id, read with a consumer group, and don't add partitions to the topic later
No key, so the sticky partitioner keeps related records together
Key by account id and read with a share group, so more members can work at once
Any key, as long as the producer has idempotence on
quiz.why: The key picks the partition, a partition keeps order, and a consumer group gives each partition to one member, so one reader handles one account's payments in order. Adding partitions later sends a key's new records to a different partition. Records without a key spread over partitions, a share group gives up order across members, and idempotence only stops a producer's own retries from repeating or reordering records.

quiz.q: A payment reader writes to a database and then commits its offset. It crashes between the two. What does the restart do, and what makes that safe?
options: It skips the payment; nothing is needed
It handles the payment again; the idempotent producer removes the repeat
Nothing, because Kafka transactions cover the database write
It handles the payment again; an idempotency key checked in the same database transaction makes the repeat harmless
quiz.why: Committing after the work is at-least-once: the restart begins at the committed offset and repeats the payment. The idempotent producer only drops a producer's own retries, and a Kafka transaction covers Kafka writes and bookmarks, not a database. The reader must recognize the repeat itself, by a key the database checks.

quiz.q: A group of three members reads six partitions with `group.protocol=consumer`, the new rebalance protocol. A fourth member joins. Which partitions stop being read during the rebalance?
options: All six, until the new assignment arrives
Only the two that move to the new member, while they move
None, because the new member only takes partitions nobody owns
Only the partitions of the group leader
quiz.why: Six partitions over four members is 2, 2, 1, 1, so two of the old members each give up one partition. Under the new protocol each member catches up on its own: the two owners give back just those partitions, commit, and the coordinator hands them to the newcomer. The rest never pause. Stopping all six is eager rebalancing, which the old protocol's default assignor list gives you.

quiz.q: One partition's lag climbs while the other eleven stay at 0. The ledger's code throws `NumberFormatException` on one record every time. What should the reader do?
options: Raise `max.poll.interval.ms` so it has time to get through the record
Catch the exception, log it and commit past the record
Send the record to a dead-letter topic with its origin in headers, wait for the ack, commit past it, and park the account's later payments behind it
Add partitions so the record moves elsewhere
quiz.why: The record fails the same way every time, so more time changes nothing, and logging and committing loses a payment. A dead-letter topic written before the commit gets the record out of the partition without losing it, and parking the account stops its later payments from overtaking it. Adding partitions doesn't move records that are already written.

quiz.q: A fee program reads `payments` and writes `fees` in Kafka transactions, and also posts each fee to a billing service over the internet inside the loop. A commit times out, and the program aborts and retries the batch. What is true afterwards?
options: `read_committed` readers see each fee once in `fees`, but the billing service got the retried calls too, unless it spots repeats by an idempotency key
The abort undid the billing calls
`fees` holds repeats for every reader
Kafka 4.4's two-phase commit made the billing service part of the transaction
quiz.why: The transaction makes the `fees` records and the input bookmark one write, so `read_committed` readers see each fee once; the aborted copies stay in the log for `read_uncommitted` readers. The calls over the internet are outside Kafka and ran again on the retry. KIP-939 hasn't shipped, and it was designed for databases, not for services called over the internet.

quiz.q: A topic has 6 partitions. Which kind of group can make good use of 20 members, each handling one record at a time?
options: A consumer group: the broker splits each partition between members
A share group: every member reads every partition, and the broker hands out records one by one
Both, with `group.protocol=consumer`
Neither: 6 is the limit for any group
quiz.why: A consumer group gives each partition to one member, so 14 of the 20 would sit idle, whatever the protocol. A share group has no such limit, at the price of order. The new consumer protocol changes how partitions are shared out, not how many owners a partition has.

quiz.q: The payout program restarts. Payments sent while it was down went to Redis in two ways: with `PUBLISH` on a channel, and with `XADD` to a stream it reads through a consumer group. What does it find when it comes back?
options: Both sets of messages, because Redis keeps them until every reader has them
Neither: Redis drops everything for a client that disconnects
Nothing from the channel, because pub/sub stored nothing; every stream entry, because the stream kept them and the group's position is still where it was
The channel's messages, but the stream entries were trimmed when it disconnected
quiz.why: Pub/sub is at-most-once: a message reaches whoever is listening at that moment, and nobody else. A stream is a log in a key: the entries stay until trimmed, and the group's last-delivered ID and pending entries survive the restart, so `XREADGROUP ... >` returns what arrived meanwhile. Entries the program held but never acknowledged are still pending under its name.
